lessons.title: Where Does the Money Go? Monthly Cash Flow
objectives: Convert pay from any pay frequency to an average monthly amount.
Calculate monthly cash flow and interpret a surplus or deficit.
Build a sinking fund for irregular expenses.
lessons.hook: Show two fictional friends who each earn $3,000 per month. One ends every month stressed; the other has $250 left. Ask: “What could be different besides income?”

notes.body: Cash flow = money in − money out for a period. Positive = surplus; negative = deficit. Use take-home (net) pay, because withholding never reaches your account.
Weekly × 52 ÷ 12; biweekly × 26 ÷ 12; semimonthly × 2; annual ÷ 12. Biweekly workers get 26 checks, so “two checks a month” undercounts by about 2 checks per year.
Annual or semiannual bills (insurance, registration, gifts) are real monthly costs. Divide each by the number of months it covers and set that amount aside every month — a sinking fund.

examples.problem: Lena’s biweekly take-home pay is $1,240. Her monthly expenses total $2,610. Find her monthly cash flow.
steps: Surplus, but small — one surprise bill could erase it.

examples.problem: Lena also pays $720 for car insurance every 6 months and $132 for renters insurance each year. What is her monthly sinking-fund amount, and what is her true cash flow?
examples.answer: Lena actually runs a $54.33 monthly deficit.

discussion: Why might someone feel “broke” even when their paycheck is larger than their monthly bills?
What is the difference between saving money and having a surplus?
Which expenses are hardest to remember when building a budget?
misconceptions: Budgeting with gross pay.
Ask students to find the deposit amount on a pay stub; that is the budget number.
Assuming biweekly = twice a month.
Count paydays on a printed calendar to show 26.
Ignoring annual bills.
Have students list every bill they know of that is not monthly.
reflection: Which irregular expenses would show up in your future budget?
How would you know whether your budget is working after three months?
lessons.extension: Research two irregular costs for a car owner in your area and build a sinking-fund plan.

support: Provide a conversion table for pay frequencies.
extend: Have students model a month with three paychecks.
Ask students to write a rule for when a biweekly worker’s surplus is real.

lessons.realWorld: Many banks and budgeting apps categorize transactions automatically; students should still check the totals against their own plan.

lessons.title: Fixed vs. Variable, Needs vs. Wants
objectives: Classify expenses as fixed or variable and as needs or wants.
Use averages to plan for variable expenses.
Compare a spending pattern with the 50/30/20 guideline and judge whether differences are reasonable.
lessons.hook: Card sort: 16 expense cards. Pairs sort them two ways (fixed/variable, need/want) and defend tough cases like a phone plan or a car.

notes.body: Fixed/variable asks “does the amount change?” Need/want asks “is it required for basic living or earning income?” A streaming subscription is fixed but a want; groceries are variable but a need.
Average several months, then add a 5–10% buffer. Track actual spending to adjust.
Needs about 50%, wants about 30%, savings/extra debt payments about 20% of take-home pay. Use it to start a conversation, not as a law.

examples.problem: Groceries were $318, $356, $341, $305. Budget the average plus 10%.
Take-home pay $3,200; needs $1,890; wants $910. Compare to 50/30/20.
steps: Needs 59.1% vs 50%; wants 28.4% vs 30%; savings 12.5% vs 20%
examples.answer: Needs are high; savings are $240 below the 20% reference ($640).

discussion: Is a car a need or a want? What information decides it?
Why might someone in an expensive city reasonably exceed 50% for needs?
Which is easier to change quickly: fixed or variable expenses?
misconceptions: Fixed means “necessary.”
Show fixed wants (subscriptions) and variable needs (groceries).
50/30/20 is a requirement.
Compare three fictional people with different rents and goals.
reflection: Which of your current spending categories are variable wants?
What percent of a future paycheck would you want to save, and why?
lessons.extension: Students design an alternative guideline (e.g., 60/20/20) for a high-cost city and justify it.

extend: Compute the dollar change needed to reach 20% savings and propose two plans.

lessons.realWorld: Credit-card and bank apps often label categories; their labels do not decide what is a need.

lessons.title: Living Within Limits: Modeling Financial Constraints
objectives: Write and solve inequalities that model budget constraints.
Determine time or hours needed to reach a savings goal.
Set and justify an emergency-fund target.
lessons.hook: “Your dream apartment is $1,450. Can you afford it?” Students list what they would need to know.

notes.body: Spending + saving ≤ income. “At most” → ≤; “at least” → ≥. Solve for the unknown and interpret the boundary.
Hours worked and months saved round UP; maximum spending amounts round DOWN to the cent.
Commonly 3–6 months of essential expenses. Start with a smaller first target (e.g., $1,000) to build momentum.

examples.problem: Gross pay $4,200/month. Rent must be ≤ 30% of gross. Max rent?
Take-home $2,900; fixed $1,760; save at least $250. Max variable spending v?
Need $1,150 more; earn $15.84 after taxes per hour. Hours?

discussion: Why might two lenders or landlords use different affordability rules?
What happens to the constraint if income is irregular (tips, gig work)?
misconceptions: Rounding hours down.
Test the rounded answer: does 72 hours reach the goal?
Flipping the inequality.
Translate the words first: “at most” means the value can equal or be below.
reflection: What constraint matters most in your life right now?
How large should your first emergency fund be, and why?
lessons.extension: Model irregular gig income with a minimum and maximum month; find a budget that works for the minimum.

extend: System of constraints: rent ≤ 30% of gross AND total housing ≤ 40% of take-home.

lessons.realWorld: Landlords often require gross income of 2.5–3× the rent; this is the same inequality from the landlord’s side.

lessons.title: Is It Worth It? Comparing Spending Decisions
objectives: Compare options using unit price, break-even analysis, and annualized cost.
Identify opportunity costs, including non-monetary ones.
Evaluate sales, BNPL offers, and subscriptions critically.
lessons.hook: Show a fictional ad: “Save $60! Today only!” Ask: “When does buying this save money, and when does it cost money?”

notes.body: Price × times per week × 52. Seeing the yearly number makes the opportunity cost visible.
Fixed cost ÷ savings per use = uses needed before the fixed option is cheaper.
Price ÷ quantity. Only a deal if you will use it all and can afford the larger up-front cost.
Compare the total paid (including fees and interest), not just the per-payment amount.

discussion: Is spending $1,495 a year on coffee a bad decision? Who gets to decide?
Why do stores place items near checkout?
What is the opportunity cost of time spent comparison shopping?
misconceptions: A lower payment means a lower price.
Compute the total of all payments.
Sales always save money.
Ask whether the purchase was planned.
reflection: Name one recurring purchase you make. What is its annual cost?
Describe a time a “deal” cost you more than expected.
lessons.extension: Research a real store’s BNPL terms (late fees, autopay) and summarize the risks.

extend: Include time value: compare saving the money at 4% APY for 5 years.
